samasa.vigraha: शस्त्रं च अनलश्च तोयौघश्च, एतेषां समाहारः, तस्मात्
samasa.type: samāhāra dvandva (its last member तोयौघ is a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa: तोयस्य ओघः)
samasa.literal: from weapon, fire and flood of water
samasa.sense: from any of the three dangers: weapons, fire, floods
samasa.alt: Also readable as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa over a dvandva, शस्त्रानलतोयानाम् ओघः, ‘an onrush of weapons, fire and water’; the singular ending fits either. The dvandva gives three distinct dangers, as the verse lists distinct sources of fear.

morph.note: The taddhita affix तसिल् (-तः) forms indeclinables with the sense of the ablative: शत्रुतः = शत्रोः ‘from an enemy’. Likewise दस्युतः and राजतः (राजन् loses its n before the affix).
Future of सम् + √भू, ‘will come about, will arise’; one verb for every clause of the verse.

mantras.anvaya: तस्य शत्रुतः भयं न (सम्भविष्यति), दस्युतः वा न, राजतः न, शस्त्रानलतोयौघात् (च भयं) कदाचित् न सम्भविष्यति।
mantras.anvaya_en: One subject (भयम्), one verb (सम्भविष्यति, given at the end), and four negated sources of fear in the ablative, three of them indeclinables in -तः.
mantras.lit: For him there will be no fear from enemies, or from robbers, nor from the king; nor will (fear) ever arise from weapons, fire or floods of water.
mantras.tr: He need never fear enemies, robbers or the king, nor weapons, fire or flood.
mantras.tr_note: The future ‘there will be no fear’ is rendered as ‘he need never fear’; कदाचित् with न (‘never’) is taken with the whole verse.

comm.t: A second list of promises, of dangers from outside: enemies, robbers, the king’s anger, weapons, fire, water. The subject moves from the plural तेषाम् of 12.5 to the generic singular तस्य, ‘(any) such person’.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) calls the Goddess भयापहा (name 121), ‘remover of fear’ — the title this verse spells out danger by danger.
A modern reading: the list is the list of an ancient household’s real fears — war, theft, the arbitrary ruler, fire, flood. The promise answers the insecurity of ordinary life, not only of the soul.

sandhi.note: Final t before the nasal m may become the nasal of its class, n. The same change gives एतन्माहात्म्यं.
a + e → ai (ममैतत्); then t → n before m (एतन्माहात्म्यम्).

i before a dissimilar vowel becomes y.

samasa.sense: a means of securing well-being; in ritual language, a rite performed for blessing and protection

morph.note: Gerundive in -तव्य with the connecting इ (√पठ् is seṭ): ‘to be recited’. With a gerundive the agent stands in the instrumental (समाहितैः).
Gerundive of √श्रु with guṇa (श्रो-) and no connecting इ: ‘to be heard’.
Ablative of तद् used as a conjunction, ‘from that (cause)’: it draws the conclusion from the promises of 12.2–6.

mantras.anvaya: तस्मात् मम एतत् माहात्म्यं समाहितैः सदा भक्त्या पठितव्यं श्रोतव्यं च; तत् हि परं स्वस्त्ययनम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A command expressed by two gerundives in the passive construction (agent समाहितैः in the instrumental), followed by a nominal clause with हि giving the reason.
mantras.lit: Therefore this Māhātmya of mine is to be recited by those of collected mind, and always to be heard with devotion; for it is the supreme means of well-being.
mantras.tr: So let this account of my glory be recited with a gathered mind and always heard with devotion; for it is the highest blessing.
mantras.tr_note: The gerundives (‘is to be recited’) are rendered as exhortations (‘let … be recited’). ‘The highest blessing’ condenses परं स्वस्त्ययनम्, ‘the supreme means of welfare’.

comm.t: The conclusion of the first group of promises: because of all this (तस्मात्), the text is to be recited and heard, with attention and with devotion. The reason given is that it is a स्वस्त्ययन, a rite of blessing.

स्वस्त्ययन is a technical word for the protective and auspicious rites of the household; by calling her own Māhātmya the ‘highest svastyayana’, the Devī places its recitation among such rites — which is how the tradition uses it.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name स्वस्तिमती (name 448), ‘she who is possessed of well-being (svasti)’ — the same word for welfare that forms स्वस्त्ययन here.

flags.uncertain: Variant: for the Gita Press स्वस्त्ययनं हि तत्, GRETIL and Freund read स्वस्त्ययनं महत् (‘a great means of well-being’); corrections.json marks the reading ‘Textual Verification Required’. The Gita Press reading is analysed; the sense is hardly affected.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (its first member महामारी is a karmadhāraya: महती मारी)
samasa.literal: those whose origin is the great pestilence
samasa.sense: the afflictions that an epidemic brings
samasa.alt: Also readable as a pañcamī tatpuruṣa, महामार्याः समुद्भवाः ‘arisen from the great pestilence’, with समुद्भव as an adjective; the sense is the same.

morph.note: Optative of the causative of √शम् (शमय- with the short a that this root keeps in the causative). The optative states what the text is able to do: ‘would quell, can quell’.
उपसर्ग, from उप + √सृज्, here in its sense of ‘affliction, visitation, epidemic’ (not the grammatical ‘prefix’).

mantras.anvaya: मम माहात्म्यं महामारीसमुद्भवान् अशेषान् उपसर्गान् तथा त्रिविधम् उत्पातं तु शमयेत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A simple active sentence: subject माहात्म्यम्, verb शमयेत्, two objects (उपसर्गान् and उत्पातम्) joined by तथा.
mantras.lit: My Māhātmya would quell all calamities arising from the great pestilence, and likewise the threefold portent.
mantras.tr: My Māhātmya stills every affliction that pestilence brings, and the three kinds of evil omen.
mantras.tr_note: The optative शमयेत् (‘would quell’) is rendered as a present of capacity.

comm.t: The recitation is said to quell two kinds of danger that no human action can avert: epidemic disease and portents. महामारी, the great pestilence, will later be named as a form of the Devī herself (12.38–39), who is both the plague and its cure.

Portents (उत्पात) are traditionally divided into three kinds — the heavenly (दिव्य), the atmospheric (आन्तरिक्ष) and the earthly (भौम) — and त्रिविधम् is usually explained in this way. Recitation of the Saptaśatī as a rite of śānti in times of epidemic rests on this verse.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess सर्वव्याधिप्रशमनी (name 551), ‘she who allays all disease’, using the same verb (प्र + √शम्) as शमयेत् here.

morph.note: Passive present: √पठ् + यक् + ते. The text is the grammatical subject (एतत्) and no agent is named: ‘wherever it is recited’.
Future of वि + √मुच्: guṇa मोच्-, and च् + स becomes क्ष (c → k before s, s → ṣ after k): मोक्ष्यामि.
Abstract noun from संनिधि ‘nearness’ by the taddhita affix ष्यञ् with vṛddhi of the first vowel: ‘the state of being near, presence’. The Gita Press spells it with anusvāra (सांनिध्य).

mantras.anvaya: यत्र मम आयतने एतत् नित्यं सम्यक् पठ्यते, तत् (अहं) सदा न विमोक्ष्यामि; तत्र मे सांनिध्यं स्थितम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause of place (यत्र …) and two main clauses: a verbal one in the first person (न विमोक्ष्यामि with object तत्) and a nominal one (सांनिध्यं … स्थितम्) introduced by the correlative तत्र.
mantras.lit: In whatever shrine of mine this is properly recited daily, that (place) I will never abandon; my presence is established there.
mantras.tr: Wherever in my shrine this is rightly recited every day, that place I will never leave: there my presence abides.

comm.t: The Devī promises her permanent presence (सांनिध्य) wherever the text is recited correctly and regularly. The condition is again twofold, as in 12.2: correctness (सम्यक्) and regularity (नित्यम्).

आयतन means a temple or sanctuary, but also any dwelling; the tradition applies the verse to the household shrine as well as the temple, and understands the daily pāṭha as making the place a seat of the Goddess.
A modern reading: the promise is attached to a practice, not to a building. Presence is said to follow faithful, regular attention, wherever it is given.
